concept.title: Metadata and social sharing
concept.shortdesc: Every page carries metadata in its head, read from the DITA: the tags that link previews, catalogues and search engines read. Nothing is invented; a value the DITA does not give is left out.

conbody.p: metadataOpen GraphDublin CoreWith the default govuk.metadata=basic, each page has Open Graph tags, which decide how a link to it looks when shared; Dublin Core tags, which government and library catalogues read; and links to its own address, its neighbours in reading order and its licence. govuk.metadata=full adds one schema.org JSON-LD block to each page. govuk.metadata=no writes none of them. The print document never carries any.

section.title: What each page carries, and where it comes from

row.entry: Tags
Read from
og:title, DC.title
The topic's title. On the home page, the map's title (a bookmap's mainbooktitle).
og:description, DC.description
The topic's shortdesc, else the shortdesc in its topicref. On the home page, the map's shortdesc or the bookmap's booktitlealt.
og:locale, DC.language
The topic's xml:lang, else the map's.
website on the home page, article elsewhere.
govuk.service.name, else the map's title.
The title of the top-level entry of the navigation the page is under.
The topic's category and keyword elements. A keyword that only repeats a word of the page's title is not a tag, and each tag is written once.
article:published_time, article:modified_time

The topic's own critdates, only when govuk.dates shows dates. Dates in a bookmap's bookmeta date the book: the toolkit copies them to every topic in place of the topic's own, so the plugin reads the topic's own from its source file, and a page with none has none.
govuk.organisation, else the bookmap's publisherinformation organization, else the bookowner organization.
The publishing organisation. With govuk.metadata.persons=yes, the topic's (or the bookmap's) author elements instead.
What the footer says: Crown copyright for official branding, else govuk.footer.licence, else the bookmap's bookrights.
The Open Government Licence for official branding, else govuk.licence.url.
link rel="canonical", og:url, link rel="prev" and "next"
The page's address, and its neighbours' in reading order, under govuk.site.url. Without it they are left out, since the plugin has no other way to know the site's address.
govuk.og.image: an absolute URL, or a path under the site root, which needs govuk.site.url.
Always summary; the other values are read from the Open Graph tags.

section.title: Structured data for search engines: govuk.metadata=full
section.p: JSON-LDschema.orgstructured dataAt full, each page also has one <script type="application/ld+json"> block in its head, in the schema.org vocabulary that search engines and language-model tools read. It is written from the same facts as the tags above, so the two always agree, and it adds the tags' structure: what the page is part of, and where it sits in the publication.

row.entry: On
The block holds
The home page
A WebSite: the publication's name, description and language, its address, and its publisher.
A topic page
A TechArticle: the headline, description, language, address, keywords, licence, dates when govuk.dates allows them, the publication it is part of, and the publisher.
A task page

The TechArticle also names a HowTo as its main entity: the task's title and description, and a HowToStep for each step, named by its cmd and told by its info (the command again when there is no information).
A glossary entry's page
The TechArticle also names a DefinedTerm as its main entity: the term, its definition, and its acronyms, abbreviations, short forms and synonyms as alternative names.
A generated page (glossary, index, lists)
A WebPage, with the same facts. On the glossary page, a DefinedTermSet of every term in the glossary is its main entity.
Every page below the home page
A BreadcrumbList: the publication, each page above this one in the map, then this page, numbered from 1. A heading in the map that is not a page is left out, so the list is always contiguous.

section.p: Two limits. A glossary of more than 500 terms has no DefinedTermSet: the glossary page already lists every term, and a block as large again would double it, so the set is left out whole (a partial set would be wrong) and the build says so (GOVK020W). And no search engine currently rewards HowTo: Google withdrew its how-to results in 2023. The block is written because it describes the page accurately for tools that read it, not for how a page appears in results.

The publisher is an Organization, or a GovernmentOrganization for the official and NHS brandings, named as govuk.organisation or the bookmap says. Every value comes from the same place as its tag, and a value the DITA does not give is left out. Without govuk.site.url there are no addresses, so there is no BreadcrumbList and no address in any object, and the rest is still written.

Values are escaped for JSON, and the characters <, > and & are written as escapes as well, so a title can never close the block it is in. A data block is not script, so a Content-Security-Policy (govuk.csp) does not restrict it; CI checks that in a browser. The block holds the headline and description a reader sees and nothing that is not on the page. To see how a search engine reads a page, use its structured-data testing tool on the published address. Which of the types a search engine rewards changes, so treat it as a description of the page, not as a way to change how it appears.

section.title: A catalogue record for data publications: govuk.dcat
section.p: DCATcatalogue recorddata.gov.ukA publication that documents data, such as a data dictionary or a data standard, can also describe that data to the catalogues that harvest it. With govuk.dcat=yes (and govuk.site.url) the build writes dcat.jsonld and dcat.ttl at the site root: the same DCAT 3 record in two serialisations, written from one graph so they are the same record. The home page links both and holds the record in its head. It is off by default, because a catalogue record is a publishing act, and the publisher turns it on.

The map says what is an asset. A branch of the map declares itself with a data element named rdf:type in the topicmeta of the topicref, topichead or topicgroup that heads it. The type is the publisher's statement and is never inferred.
section.codeblock: <topicref href="elements/index.dita"> <topicmeta> <data name="rdf:type" value="dct:Standard"/> <data name="dct:identifier" value="https://example.org/dictionary/elements"/> <data name="dct:conformsTo" value="https://example.org/model"/> </topicmeta> <!-- a distribution: a data file the site ships, inside the branch --> <topicref href="schemas/return.schema.json" format="json" processing-role="resource-only"/> </topicref>

ul.li: The type is a class of a vocabulary the plugin knows (dcat:Dataset, dcat:DataService, dct:Standard, adms:Asset) or an absolute address. One that is neither is reported (GOVK017W) and the entry is left out.

A submap is declared by wrapping its mapref in a topicgroup that carries the topicmeta. DITA-OT drops the topicmeta of the mapref itself, and of the submap file's root, when it resolves the reference.

The asset's landing page is its entry's first page. Its title and description are the entry's, else that page's. Its identifier is the address given as dct:identifier, else its landing page's address. The publisher, licence, language, rights and contact come from the publication unless the entry says otherwise. Any other property is a data element (dct:spatial, dct:temporal, dct:accrualPeriodicity, dcat:theme and so on) with the address or value the target catalogue expects.

A resource-only reference inside the branch to a file of a data type (JSON, CSV, Turtle, YAML, XML, a spreadsheet, a zip) is the asset's distribution. The build publishes the file at its path, and the record links it there with its media type and format.
One declared asset gives that asset, with no catalogue around it. Several give a catalogue of them. None gives no record, and the build says so (GOVK018W).
govuk.contact.email adds an organisational contact point. It is never a person by default.

section.p: What data.gov.uk expects. A title, a description, a stable identifier and a licence. A record that lacks one is still written, and the build names the property and the record (GOVK019W), so the harvester will not be the first to say so.

Model honestly. A documentation site describes data; it is not the data. A data standard, a logical model or a data set specification is a dct:Standard. An interface is a dcat:DataService. Declare dcat:Dataset only for a branch that ships or links the data itself, and give it the files as distributions. A dictionary that holds many specifications is a catalogue of standards, not a dataset.

To check a built site, tools/check_metadata.py verifies the mandatory properties and that every reference in the record names a record in it, and tools/check_rdf.py parses both files with an independent RDF library and confirms they are the same graph.

section.title: Any other property: data elements
section.p: metadatadata elementA <data name="prefix:term" value="…"/> in a bookmap's bookmeta, the topicmeta of a map or an entry, or a topic's prolog states a property in a published vocabulary. The prefixes are dct (Dublin Core terms), dcat, adms, skos, rdf, foaf, org, vcard, schema and og.

ul.li: A property reaches every tag that is read from it. The example adds an article:tag.
A correct term that nothing at this level reads, such as dct:spatial, is kept for the catalogue outputs to come, and is not written.
A name that is not a term of those vocabularies, such as a misspelt dct:spacial, is reported once per build (GOVK011W) and left out.
A data element whose name has no prefix is the publisher's own, and is not metadata.

section.p: A page states its own properties first, from the entries above it in the map and then from its prolog. It takes the rest from the publication, except the properties that describe one thing only: its title, description, identifier, type, subjects and dates. A system that generates DITA should follow the guide for source systems.

section.title: Checking
section.p: A page the metadata tables require a value for, and that has none, is reported once per build for all such pages (GOVK012W). To look at a published page as a link preview will, use a social network's sharing debugger, or read the page's source. The repository's tools/check_metadata.py checks a built site against the same tables offline. It runs from wherever it is kept: it takes the tables from the plugin installed in the toolkit the dita command belongs to, from DITA_HOME, or from the toolkit named with --dita-dir; --tables names the plugin's resource/metadata folder directly. When it cannot find them it says where it looked and exits with status 2.

section.title: An index for language models: llms.txt
section.p: llms.txtlanguage modelsWhen govuk.site.url is set, the build writes llms.txt at the site root beside sitemap.xml. It follows the llms.txt convention: a short Markdown index that a language model, or an agent reading the site, can use instead of crawling it. govuk.llms=no turns it off.

It holds the publication's title and description, then a section for each top-level entry in the map, listing its pages with the titles and short descriptions the home page shows, each linked by its full address. The pages are the sitemap's: topics that are resource-only or toc="no", the search page and the print document are left out. The glossary, index and list pages come last, under Optional, which a reader short of room may skip.
section.codeblock:
# GOV.UK DITA plugin manual
> How to install and use org.istanduk.gov-uk, …
## Getting started
- [Installing the plugin](https://example.org/manual/topics/install.html): Install the plugin …
section.p: What it does and does not do. A minority of sites publish one, and as of October 2026 no major AI company says its systems read it; the main web crawlers rarely ask for it. The tools that do read it are mostly coding assistants and documentation tools that are pointed at a site. The plugin writes it because it costs nothing and lists only what the site already publishes, not because it is known to help.

robots.txtIf you do not want your content used to train AI models, llms.txt is the wrong tool: leaving it out does not keep a site out of training data, and publishing it gives no permission. Set Disallow rules in robots.txt for the crawlers you want to exclude (each AI company documents its crawler's name), and say what reuse you allow in your licence. The robots.txt the plugin writes beside the sitemap allows every crawler; ship your own in the output folder and the plugin leaves it alone.

The convention also suggests a Markdown copy of every page, and a full-text llms-full.txt. The plugin writes neither: its pages are HTML, and the print document already holds the whole publication. A separate toolkit plugin, fox.jason.llms.txt, makes Markdown output if you need it.
